q: What's the bias on FOODS_3?
answer: FOODS_3 has a signed bias of -0.7%, i.e. slight under-forecasting (the model predicts marginally fewer units than sold) over the 263-day backtest. That is close to zero, so there's no meaningful systematic over- or under-stocking signal at the department level. Read it alongside accuracy though: FOODS_3 forecast accuracy is 80.1% versus 87.1% for the seasonal-naive baseline, so near-zero bias here is coming from offsetting daily errors rather than from tight day-to-day fit.

q: What is the forecast accuracy for HOUSEHOLD_1?
answer: HOUSEHOLD_1's forecast accuracy is 78.3% over the 263-day backtest — but that number is misleading on its own: the seasonal-naive baseline scored 87.8% on the same department. Forecast value add is -9.4 pp, so the model does not beat naive here; simply repeating last week's same weekday would have been more accurate.

q: What's the forecast value add on HOBBIES_2?
answer: HOBBIES_2 has a forecast value add of +10.6 pp — the model beats the seasonal-naive baseline. That comes from 65.6% forecast accuracy vs 54.9% for the naive baseline. Caveat on materiality: HOBBIES_2 is the smallest department in the backtest at 6,227 units over the 263-day window, and both accuracy levels are low in absolute terms, so this large edge applies to a very small slice of volume.

q: What's the overall forecast value add, pooled across all departments?
answer: Pooled across all seven departments, forecast value add is -5.7 pp — the model is destroying accuracy versus the baseline. Model FA is 79.5% against a seasonal-naive FA of 85.2% over the 263-day backtest (1,153,225 units). Only 2 of 7 departments beat the naive baseline. Pooled bias is small at -0.3% (slight under-forecast), so the problem is error dispersion, not systematic level.

q: How many units did FOODS_1 sell over the whole backtest window?
answer: FOODS_1 sold 86,718 units over the 263-day backtest window. That makes it the fifth-largest of the seven departments by volume (for scale, FOODS_3 leads with 615,655 units).

q: Is the model over-forecasting or under-forecasting HOUSEHOLD_2, and by how much?
answer: HOUSEHOLD_2 is over-forecast: signed bias is +3.0% over the 263-day backtest, i.e. the model predicts about 3% more units than actually sold. For context, its forecast accuracy is 79.0% against a seasonal-naive baseline of 86.6%, so the small bias sits alongside a fairly weak overall accuracy for this department.

q: What share of revenue do the top 20% of SKUs account for?
answer: The top 20% of SKUs account for 56.0% of realised revenue (ranked by the revenue-weighted seasonal priority score, across all 3,049 SKUs in the backtest).

q: What was Prophet's WAPE on HOBBIES_2?
answer: Prophet's WAPE on HOBBIES_2 was 34.32% (daily data). For context, the Elastic Net benchmark on the same department shows 58.96% WAPE, but that was run on monthly aggregates, so the two figures are not directly comparable head-to-head. HOBBIES_2 is a low-volume department, averaging 23.6 units/day.

q: How many units did FOODS_1 actually sell on the last day of the backtest, and what did the model predict?
answer: On the last day of the backtest, 2014-01-22, FOODS_1 sold 180 units while the model predicted 298.6 units — an absolute error of 118.6 units (the seasonal-naive baseline predicted 200.0 units, much closer). Note the model output was flat at 298.6 units across the final three days while actuals fell from 334 to 180, so it badly over-forecast the end-of-window decline.

q: Which departments beat the seasonal naive baseline?
answer: Only 2 of 7 departments beat the seasonal-naive baseline: HOBBIES_2 (+10.6 pp FVA) and HOBBIES_1 (+2.8 pp FVA). The other five are negative — FOODS_2 -0.9 pp, FOODS_3 -7.0 pp, FOODS_1 -7.3 pp, HOUSEHOLD_2 -7.6 pp, HOUSEHOLD_1 -9.4 pp. Caveat on weight: the biggest winner, HOBBIES_2, is the smallest department at 6,227 units over the window, while the losers include FOODS_3 (615,655 units) and HOUSEHOLD_1 (163,737 units). Pooled across all departments the model is behind the baseline: 79.5% forecast accuracy vs 85.2% naive, i.e. -5.7 pp FVA.

q: Which department has the worst forecast value add?
answer: HOUSEHOLD_1 has the worst forecast value add: -9.4 pp. Its model accuracy is 78.3% against a seasonal-naive baseline of 87.8%, so simply repeating last week's same weekday would have been substantially more accurate. It also matters: at 163,737 units it is the second-largest department by volume. For context, the next worst are HOUSEHOLD_2 (-7.6 pp) and FOODS_1 (-7.3 pp), and only 2 of 7 departments beat the baseline (pooled FVA -5.7 pp).

q: Which department has the highest standalone forecast accuracy?
answer: HOBBIES_1 has the highest standalone forecast accuracy at 82.2%, ahead of FOODS_3 (80.1%) and FOODS_2 (79.3%). Read it next to its baseline: HOBBIES_1's seasonal-naive accuracy is 79.3%, so the model does add value there (+2.8 pp FVA). Worth noting that standalone FA and value add do not line up — HOBBIES_2 has the lowest FA of the seven (65.6%) yet the largest FVA (+10.6 pp), because its naive baseline is much harder to beat than HOBBIES_1's.

q: Which department has the biggest bias problem in either direction?
answer:
By raw magnitude, HOBBIES_2 has the worst bias: -7.5% (under-forecasting), the largest of the seven departments. But it is the smallest department in the backtest at 6,227 units, so the absolute exposure is small; its accuracy is also the weakest (FA 65.6% vs naive 54.9%).

Weighted by volume, the more consequential bias problem is FOODS_2: -4.2% under-forecast on 113,746 units, and it is the only one of these where the model also trails the baseline (FA 79.3% vs naive 80.2%). HOUSEHOLD_1 is the largest over-forecaster at +4.1% on 163,737 units. The biggest department, FOODS_3 (615,655 units), is essentially unbiased at -0.7%.

Scoping note: bias here is signed total-forecast vs total-actual over the full 263-day window, and near-zero bias can still hide offsetting daily errors.

q: Rank the three FOODS departments by forecast value add.
answer: All three FOODS departments have negative forecast value add — the seasonal-naive baseline beat the model in every one. Ranked best (least bad) to worst: 1) FOODS_2 at -0.9 pp (FA 79.3% vs naive 80.2%); 2) FOODS_3 at -7.0 pp (FA 80.1% vs naive 87.1%); 3) FOODS_1 at -7.3 pp (FA 75.0% vs naive 82.2%). Note FOODS_3 is by far the largest department (615,655 units over the 263-day window), so its -7.0 pp shortfall carries the most weight even though FOODS_1 ranks marginally lower.

q: Compare the forecast accuracy of FOODS_1 and FOODS_2 against their naive baselines.
answer:
Both departments lose to the seasonal-naive baseline, but FOODS_1 loses far more badly.

FOODS_1: forecast accuracy 75.0% vs naive 82.2% — a forecast value add of -7.3 pp (does not beat naive), on 86,718 units.
FOODS_2: forecast accuracy 79.3% vs naive 80.2% — a forecast value add of -0.9 pp (does not beat naive), on 113,746 units.

So FOODS_2's model is essentially at parity with simply repeating last week's same weekday, while FOODS_1's model is clearly worse than the free baseline and is the more urgent fix of the two.

q: On which department did Elastic Net do worse than Prophet?
answer: HOBBIES_2 is the only department where Elastic Net's WAPE is higher than Prophet's: Elastic Net 58.96% (monthly) vs Prophet 34.32% (daily). In every other department the Elastic Net figure is the lower of the two (e.g. FOODS_3 4.86% vs 19.81%, HOUSEHOLD_1 3.26% vs 21.56%, HOBBIES_1 4.32% vs 18.57%, FOODS_2 5.31% vs 20.55%, FOODS_1 6.96% vs 24.99%, HOUSEHOLD_2 8.99% vs 20.94%). Important caveat: the two WAPEs are not directly comparable — Prophet was scored on daily units and Elastic Net on monthly aggregates, and monthly aggregation cancels noise. So the only meaningful reading is that HOBBIES_2 stands out: Elastic Net is worse there even with the aggregation advantage, which fits its very thin volume (mean 23.6 units/day).

q: Of the departments losing to the naive baseline, which has the highest volume?
answer: FOODS_3. Five of the seven departments have negative forecast value add (FOODS_2 -0.9pp, FOODS_3 -7.0pp, FOODS_1 -7.3pp, HOUSEHOLD_2 -7.6pp, HOUSEHOLD_1 -9.4pp), and FOODS_3 is by far the largest of them at 615,655 units over the 263-day window — roughly the volume of all other departments combined. Its forecast accuracy is 80.1% versus 87.1% for the seasonal-naive baseline, so the model is actively worse than repeating last week's same weekday on the store's biggest department. The next-largest loser, HOUSEHOLD_1 (163,737 units), has the worst FVA at -9.4pp and is the second priority.

q: Which departments is the model losing to the naive baseline, and why might that be?
answer:
Five of the seven departments lose to the seasonal-naive baseline: HOUSEHOLD_1 (FVA -9.4pp), HOUSEHOLD_2 (-7.6pp), FOODS_1 (-7.3pp), FOODS_3 (-7.0pp) and FOODS_2 (-0.9pp, essentially a tie). Only HOBBIES_2 (+10.6pp) and HOBBIES_1 (+2.8pp) add value; pooled FVA is -5.7pp (79.5% model vs 85.2% naive), with 2 of 7 departments beating naive.

Why, as far as the data shows:
(1) The losses cluster exactly where the naive baseline is strongest. Naive accuracy is 87.8% in HOUSEHOLD_1, 87.1% in FOODS_3 and 86.6% in HOUSEHOLD_2 — stable, strongly weekly demand that 'repeat last week's same weekday' already captures, leaving little headroom. Conversely the model's big win, HOBBIES_2, is where naive is weakest (54.9%).
(2) It is not a level/bias problem: signed bias is small in the losing departments (FOODS_3 -0.7%, HOUSEHOLD_2 +3.0%, FOODS_1 -3.9%, HOUSEHOLD_2/HOUSEHOLD_1 +4.1%, FOODS_2 -4.2%), and pooled bias is -0.3%. The gap is in day-to-day shape, not average level.
(3) The model looks over-smoothed and drifts out of date. FOODS_3's worst days are spikes and a closure the flat model misses — 2013-12-25 (actual 0, model 2431.5), 2013-08-25 (actual 4042, model 2497.5, naive error only 642 units) and 2013-09-08 (actual 3960, model 2497.5, naive error 209 units): the model prints nearly the same number each day while naive tracks the moving level. That degradation grows over the backtest in HOUSEHOLD_1 (FVA -5.0pp in fold 1 vs -12.3pp in fold 3; FOODS_3 -6.0pp to -7.1pp).
The weight matters: FOODS_3 (615,655 units) and HOUSEHOLD_1 (163,737 units) are the two largest departments, so their negative FVA drives the pooled result.

q: Take the department with the worst forecast value add — is its bias over or under, and how big?
answer: Worst FVA is HOUSEHOLD_1 at -9.4 pp, and it over-forecasts by +4.1% (predicting more units than sold, i.e. excess-stock risk). Context: its forecast accuracy is 78.3% versus 87.8% for the seasonal-naive baseline, so repeating last week's same weekday would have been more accurate. Note bias near zero can hide offsetting daily errors — here the modest +4.1% bias sits alongside a sizeable accuracy shortfall, so the problem is day-to-day error, not just a level shift.

q: For the only department where the model beats naive by double digits, what does its last week of daily actuals vs model look like?
answer: The only department beating naive by double digits is HOBBIES_2 (+10.6 pp FVA; 65.6% forecast accuracy vs 54.9% naive). Its last week of data (2014-01-16 to 2014-01-22) looks like this — actual units vs model units (abs error): Jan 16: 19 vs 27.6 (8.6); Jan 17: 13 vs 27.6 (14.6); Jan 18: 20 vs 27.6 (7.6); Jan 19: 19 vs 27.6 (8.6); Jan 20: 28 vs 27.6 (0.4); Jan 21: 21 vs 27.6 (6.6); Jan 22: 12 vs 27.6 (15.6). Two things stand out. First, the model is completely flat at 27.6 units every day — it carries no day-of-week shape at all in this window, so its 'win' comes from being a stable average against a very noisy series (naive ranged from 12 to 42 units over the same week). Second, over these seven days actuals ran 12-28 units, mostly below 27.6, so the model over-shot on six of seven days, even though its full-backtest bias is -7.5% (under-forecasting). This is also the smallest department in the store at 6,227 units over 263 days, so the double-digit edge is on very low volume.

q: Is the model's weekly accuracy getting better or worse toward the end of the backtest, compared to the naive baseline?
answer: Worse. Pooled across all seven departments, the model trails the seasonal-naive baseline for most of the 38 weeks, and the gap widens toward the end. Early on the shortfall was small (week of 2013-05-06: 82.3% model vs 84.4% naive; 2013-05-13: 85.0% vs 86.4%), and the model even led in a few weeks (2013-07-22: 89.5% vs 89.2%; 2013-12-02: 83.0% vs 72.7%; 2013-12-30: 84.1% vs 73.9% — the holiday weeks where the naive baseline breaks down). But the final three weeks are the weakest stretch relative to baseline: 2014-01-06 79.9% vs 83.6%, 2014-01-13 76.0% vs 87.4%, and 2014-01-20 68.8% vs 89.9% — the naive baseline recovers to near its best level while model accuracy falls to its lowest outside Christmas week (2013-12-23: 66.3%). For context, the full-window pooled result is 79.5% model vs 85.2% naive, a forecast value add of -5.7 pp, with only 2 of 7 departments beating naive. Scope: this is the pooled weekly trend, not department-level; note the last row may be a partial week at the end of the window.

q: Of the two departments that beat the naive baseline, which one has more volume, and what is its forecast accuracy?
answer: HOBBIES_1 is the larger of the two departments that beat the baseline. The two winners are HOBBIES_2 (FVA +10.6 pp) and HOBBIES_1 (FVA +2.8 pp); HOBBIES_1 sold 121,662 units over the 263-day window versus just 6,227 for HOBBIES_2. HOBBIES_1's forecast accuracy is 82.2%, against a seasonal-naive accuracy of 79.3%. Note the win is modest and confined to a mid-sized department — pooled across all seven departments the model still trails the baseline (79.5% vs 85.2%, -5.7 pp).

q: Does the department with the worst Prophet WAPE also have the worst forecast value add?
answer: No — they are opposite ends. The worst Prophet daily WAPE belongs to HOBBIES_2 (34.32%), but HOBBIES_2 has the *best* forecast value add of the seven departments (+10.6 pp). The worst FVA is HOUSEHOLD_1 (-9.4 pp), whose Prophet WAPE is 21.56% — mid-pack, and far better than HOBBIES_2's. The reason is that FVA is relative to the seasonal-naive baseline: HOBBIES_2 is a tiny, erratic department (23.6 mean daily units) where absolute error is high but the naive baseline is even worse, while HOUSEHOLD_1 is a smooth series that the naive baseline handles well. Caveat: the Prophet WAPE comes from a separate model-comparison benchmark and is not directly comparable to the planning-view accuracy figures behind FVA.

q: How's the forecast doing?
answer:
Short version: the model is losing to the seasonal-naive baseline. Pooled across all 7 departments over the 263-day backtest, forecast accuracy is 79.5% versus 85.2% for the naive baseline — an FVA of -5.7pp. Bias is essentially neutral at -0.3%, so the problem is error size, not systematic over/under-forecasting.

Only 2 of 7 departments beat naive: HOBBIES_2 (+10.6pp) and HOBBIES_1 (+2.8pp). The losers include the biggest volume drivers: FOODS_3 (-7.0pp, 615,655 units — over half of the 1,153,225 total) and HOUSEHOLD_1 (-9.4pp, 163,737 units). HOBBIES_2, the best performer, is the smallest department at 6,227 units, so its win barely moves the pooled number.

Recent weeks don't show a turnaround: in the last 8 weeks the model trailed naive in 6 of them, ending the week of 2014-01-20 at 68.8% vs 89.9% naive.

q: Is the model any good?
answer:
Short answer: no — not as it stands. Pooled across all 7 departments over the 263-day backtest, the model hits 79.5% forecast accuracy versus 85.2% for a seasonal-naive baseline (just repeating last week's same weekday), i.e. forecast value add of -5.7pp. Only 2 of 7 departments beat naive.

Where it works: HOBBIES_2 (+10.6pp FVA) and HOBBIES_1 (+2.8pp). But HOBBIES_2 is tiny (6,227 units), so the win carries little weight; HOBBIES_1 at 121,662 units is the one genuinely useful case.

Where it hurts: the big volume sits where the model loses. FOODS_3 (615,655 units) is -7.0pp and HOUSEHOLD_1 (163,737 units) is -9.4pp; HOUSEHOLD_2 -7.6pp, FOODS_1 -7.3pp, FOODS_2 -0.9pp.

One thing in its favour: bias is essentially neutral at -0.3% pooled, so it isn't systematically over- or under-forecasting. And it does hold up better in disrupted weeks — in the weeks starting 2013-11-25, 2013-12-02 and 2013-12-30 it beat naive (e.g. 84.1% vs 73.9%), but in calm weeks naive wins outright (week of 2014-01-20: 68.8% vs 89.9%).

Verdict: usable only for HOBBIES_1/HOBBIES_2 and possibly for holiday-disrupted periods; for the high-volume food and household lines the naive baseline is the better default today.

q: What's the accuracy?
answer: Scoped as overall accuracy, pooled across all seven departments over the 263-day backtest: forecast accuracy is 79.5%. But read next to the baseline, that's a poor result — the seasonal-naive baseline scored 85.2%, so the model's value add is -5.7 percentage points, and only 2 of 7 departments beat naive. Bias is essentially neutral at -0.3%. By department, FA ranges from 82.2% (HOBBIES_1) down to 65.6% (HOBBIES_2), with FOODS_3 at 80.1%, FOODS_2 79.3%, HOUSEHOLD_2 79.0%, HOUSEHOLD_1 78.3%, FOODS_1 75.0%. Tell me if you meant a specific department or window and I'll pull that figure.

q: Where should we focus?
answer:
Scoped as: where to focus forecast-improvement effort across the 7 departments in this backtest. Headline: the model is losing to the seasonal-naive baseline overall — 79.5% forecast accuracy vs 85.2% naive, i.e. -5.7pp value add, with only 2 of 7 departments beating naive. So the first focus is fixing the model, not tuning it.

Priority 1 — FOODS_3: 615,655 units (over half of the 1,153,225 total) and -7.0pp value add (80.1% vs 87.1% naive). Biggest volume plus a large deficit, and it isn't improving: fold 1 was -6.0pp, fold 3 -7.1pp. Bias is essentially clean (-0.7%), so the problem is day-to-day pattern, not level.

Priority 2 — HOUSEHOLD_1: worst value add of all (-9.4pp; 78.3% vs 87.8% naive) on the second-largest volume (163,737 units), with +4.1% over-forecast bias.

Deprioritise: HOBBIES_2 has the best value add (+10.6pp) but only 6,227 units, and HOBBIES_1 (+2.8pp) is already the most accurate department at 82.2%. FOODS_2 is near-neutral (-0.9pp).

One caveat: recent weeks look weak too — in the week starting 2014-01-20 the model ran 68.8% vs 89.9% naive — so treat baseline-replacement for the high-volume food and household lines as urgent.

There is no forward-looking forecast output for any future period, so I can't give you next-quarter demand numbers. q: Since Elastic Net's WAPE is 4x better than Prophet's, should we switch all departments to Elastic Net?
answer:
The premise doesn't hold, so the switch decision can't be made on that basis. Two problems:

1) The two WAPEs are measured on different things. Prophet was scored on daily units; Elastic Net on monthly aggregates. Monthly aggregation cancels day-to-day noise, so a lower monthly WAPE is expected mechanically and is not evidence Elastic Net is more accurate. The study itself flags that the two are not directly comparable.

2) Even taken at face value, the gap is not uniform and not always in Elastic Net's favour. Prophet daily vs Elastic Net monthly WAPE: FOODS_3 19.81 vs 4.86, HOUSEHOLD_1 21.56 vs 3.26, HOBBIES_1 18.57 vs 4.32, FOODS_2 20.55 vs 5.31, FOODS_1 24.99 vs 6.96, HOUSEHOLD_2 20.94 vs 8.99 — but HOBBIES_2 reverses, 34.32 vs 58.96, with Elastic Net far worse on the smallest department (23.6 mean daily units).

Also note the decision depends on the horizon you actually plan at. If replenishment needs daily units, a monthly-aggregate model doesn't answer the question at all. A fair test would score both models at the same granularity; that test is not in this backtest.

Separately, for context on the planning model in production: pooled forecast accuracy is 79.5% vs 85.2% for seasonal-naive (FVA -5.7pp), with only 2 of 7 departments beating naive — so the more urgent question is whether the current model earns its keep against the baseline at all.
